common_name: Alexandrina Magnolia (Classic Large Pink-Purple Saucer Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Alexandrina is among the earliest-blooming saucer magnolia cultivars, so a sheltered site away from cold pockets helps protect the flowers from late frost damage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Alexandrina is one of the oldest and most widely planted saucer magnolia cultivars, producing large, goblet-shaped flowers in rich rose-purple on the outside and creamy white within, opening on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge. Its early bloom timing gives an unmistakable, showy spring display but also leaves the flowers vulnerable to browning from a late hard freeze, a common risk for early-flowering saucer magnolias, so siting away from low frost pockets helps. The tree grows into a broad, multi-stemmed small tree or large shrub with minimal pruning needs beyond removing dead or crossing wood, and established trees are otherwise low-maintenance and long-lived landscape specimens.

common_name: Lennei Magnolia (Full-Petaled Deep Purple-Pink Saucer Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Lennei blooms somewhat later than Alexandrina, giving it a bit more protection from late-season frost damage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Lennei is a classic saucer magnolia cultivar valued for its unusually full, heavy-petaled flowers in a deep rose-purple on the outside with a paler, almost white interior, giving each bloom a rounded, goblet-like fullness distinct from the more open form of many other saucer magnolia cultivars. It flowers on bare branches in early to mid spring, somewhat later than Alexandrina, and grows into a broad, spreading, multi-stemmed small tree that needs little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood. Established trees are long-lived, low-maintenance landscape specimens, though a late hard freeze can still brown open flowers in an unusually cold spring.

common_name: Rustica Rubra Magnolia (Later-Blooming Rose-Red Saucer Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Rustica Rubra's later bloom time than Alexandrina and Lennei helps it dodge late frosts that damage earlier saucer magnolia cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Rustica Rubra produces deep rose-red, cup-shaped flowers with a paler interior, blooming somewhat later in spring than Alexandrina and Lennei, which gives it a real practical advantage in regions prone to late hard freezes that can blacken the open flowers of earlier saucer magnolia cultivars. The tree grows into a broad, spreading, multi-stemmed small tree or large shrub, requiring little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood, and its rich color makes it a striking spring focal point once established. Give it a sheltered site with consistent moisture for the healthiest growth and most reliable annual bloom.

common_name: Betty Magnolia (Little Girl Series Late-Blooming Reddish-Purple Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Betty is a compact 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolia from the U.S. National Arboretum, bred to bloom later than star and saucer magnolias to help avoid late-frost flower damage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Betty is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum, producing large, fragrant, deep reddish-purple, multi-petaled, tulip-shaped flowers with a paler interior on a compact, multi-stemmed tree small enough for a modest-sized yard. Like its sibling Jane, its key advantage is later bloom timing than star and saucer magnolias, helping the flowers dodge the late spring freezes that often damage earlier-blooming magnolias, and it sometimes produces a light rebloom later in the season as well. Give it a sheltered spot with consistent moisture and avoid heavy pruning, since magnolias generally need little routine shaping beyond removing dead or crossing wood.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Magnolia Breeding Program

common_name: Susan Magnolia (Little Girl Series Deep Purple-Red Compact Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Susan is one of the most popular 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias, bred to bloom later than star and saucer magnolias to help avoid late-frost flower damage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Susan is one of the most widely planted of the 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum, producing slender, elegant, deep reddish-purple buds that open into fragrant, tulip-shaped flowers on a compact, multi-stemmed tree suited to smaller gardens where a full-size saucer magnolia would eventually be too large. Its later bloom timing than star and saucer magnolias helps it avoid the late spring freezes that often damage earlier-flowering magnolias, and it is known to produce a light rebloom later in summer more reliably than some of its Little Girl siblings. Give it a sheltered spot with consistent moisture, and avoid heavy pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Magnolia Breeding Program
